reference.source: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: A rare fibrosing interstitial lung disease defined by fibrosis of the visceral pleura and subpleural parenchyma with striking upper-lobe predominance.
May be idiopathic or associated with haematopoietic stem cell or lung transplantation, recurrent infection, chemotherapy, autoimmune disease and familial pulmonary fibrosis.
A characteristic phenotype comprises a thin body habitus, a flattened thorax with reduced anteroposterior diameter (platythorax) and deepening of the suprasternal notch.
Presents with breathlessness, dry cough, recurrent pneumothoraces and weight loss.
HRCT shows dense upper-zone pleural and subpleural fibrosis with volume loss, traction bronchiectasis and architectural distortion, sparing the lower zones early in disease.
Histology demonstrates intra-alveolar fibrosis with prominent elastosis and visceral pleural thickening (elastofibrosis).
It frequently coexists with another interstitial lung disease pattern, such as UIP, in the lower lobes.
No drug therapy is of proven benefit; antifibrotic agents are being explored and transplantation is considered in suitable patients.
reference.pathophysiology: Pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis is defined by dense fibroelastotic thickening of the visceral pleura and the immediately subpleural parenchyma, with elastin-rich fibrosis obliterating alveolar spaces predominantly in the upper lobes. Proposed mechanisms include recurrent injury and infection, immune dysregulation such as after transplantation, and genetic predisposition; the upper-zone distribution and marked elastosis are distinctive.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis with a UIP pattern
Apical fibrosis following prior tuberculosis or radiation
Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease
additionalInvestigations: HRCT thorax demonstrating upper-zone pleuroparenchymal fibrosis
Pulmonary function tests, which show restriction with a characteristically preserved or raised residual volume relative to total lung capacity due to platythorax
Surgical lung biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain
Autoimmune serology and detailed exposure history
Review of prior transplant, chemotherapy or recurrent infection history
Assessment for coexistent lower-lobe interstitial lung disease
redFlags: Coexisting lower-lobe fibrosis indicating combined disease with a worse outcome
reference.prognosis: The disease is often progressive with a poor outcome, particularly when combined with lower-lobe fibrosis; pneumothorax and progressive respiratory failure are common complications.
pitfalls: Dismissing apical changes as old infection or scarring
Missing the characteristic body habitus and preserved lung volumes as diagnostic clues
Overlooking coexisting lower-lobe interstitial lung disease
Attributing recurrent pneumothorax to primary spontaneous pneumothorax
